title: Memory Stocks Sandisk and Micron Crash After Blistering First-Half Rally as AI Trade Unwinds
excerpt: After gains of 858% and 304% respectively through June, Sandisk and Micron have plunged more than 35% and 20% in July as fears of an easing AI compute shortage sparked a violent rotation.
body:
• Sandisk fell more than 35% and Micron dropped over 20% in July after recording gains of 858% and 304% respectively through the first half of 2026.
  • The sell-off was triggered by reports that Meta plans to sell spare AI computing capacity, raising fears that the AI compute shortage may be easing.
  • UBS analysts forecast DRAM supply will remain in deficit until at least Q2 2028, suggesting the fundamental demand picture remains intact despite the correction.
  • Analysts see the pullback as profit-taking after an extraordinary run rather than a signal that AI memory demand is weakening.

The Sharpest Correction of 2026

On July 2, Sandisk stock plunged 14% in a single session, closing at $1,745. Micron fell in sympathy. Samsung and SK Hynix dropped sharply in Seoul. The entire memory complex, which had been the hottest trade on Wall Street for six months, was suddenly and violently unwinding.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=OgKzg8aVv0A

The trigger came from outside the memory industry. Reports that Meta Platforms was considering selling its spare AI computing capacity to outside customers stoked fears that the AI compute shortage — the thesis undergirding the entire memory rally — might be easing. For stocks that had risen hundreds of percent in months, that was enough to spark a cascade of profit-taking.

By month's end, the damage was severe. Sandisk had fallen more than 35% from its June highs. Micron dropped over 20%. Billions in market capitalization evaporated in what became the sharpest sector correction of 2026.

A Correction, Not a Collapse

To understand the sell-off, context matters. Through June 30, Sandisk had risen 858% year-to-date. Micron was up 304%. Those are returns most investors wait decades to see, delivered in six months. At those levels, any negative signal — real or perceived — was going to trigger aggressive profit-taking.

Nothing about Sandisk's or Micron's underlying businesses changed on July 2. No earnings miss, no guidance cut, no contract cancellation. This was a sentiment reset after a red-hot run, not evidence that demand for AI memory chips had peaked.

"DRAM supply will remain in deficit globally until at least Q2 2028."

— Nicolas Gaudois, UBS analyst

The Supply-Demand Equation

The bull case for memory stocks rests on a straightforward premise: AI infrastructure requires enormous amounts of memory, and supply cannot keep up with demand. That equation has not changed. UBS analyst Nicolas Gaudois recently forecast a 32% sequential jump in DRAM prices for Q3 2026, nearly double his previous 17% estimate. He projects DRAM supply growth of 19.3% next year against demand growth of 36.2% — meaning the deficit is getting wider, not narrower.

Citi has raised its forecasts for Micron, predicting sequential DRAM price increases of up to 44% in Q2 2026, 20% in Q3, and 13% in Q4. Bank of America has reiterated its buy rating. Industry analysts at Morningstar note that NAND supply shortages are expected to persist through 2027.

The fear that sparked the sell-off — SK Hynix signaling a big jump in spending, Chinese memory makers ramping cheap supply — reflects a cyclical concern that has haunted memory investors for decades. Memory is inherently cyclical, and past booms have ended badly when supply caught up. But the scale of AI demand appears to be pushing this cycle's timeline further out than bears expected.

Where Things Stand

Memory demand is projected to generate $992 billion in industry sales this year, potentially doubling to $1.76 trillion in 2027 as both volumes and prices continue to rise. For investors who entered these stocks in January, even after the July correction the gains remain extraordinary. For those who bought near the June highs, the drawdown has been painful.

The question now is whether the July sell-off was a healthy reset that creates a buying opportunity, or the beginning of a deeper unwind. Analyst consensus leans toward the former, but with Sandisk still trading at a P/E ratio of roughly 60 — three times Micron's multiple — the valuation gap between the two memory giants may itself become a source of volatility in the months ahead.
